title: The Arizona home buying process, step by step
seoTitle: Arizona Home Buying Process, Step by Step | Teigh Wade REALTOR®
description: How buying a home in Arizona works: buyer-broker agreement, pre-approval, offer, earnest money, inspection period, BINSR, appraisal, escrow and recording.
summary: Buying a home in Arizona follows a set path: sign a buyer-broker agreement, get pre-approved, make an offer on the standard AAR contract, deposit earnest money, inspect during the inspection period, negotiate repairs on the BINSR, clear appraisal and loan conditions, review HOA documents, do a final walkthrough, sign with escrow, then fund and record.

sections.html:
Most Arizona home purchases use the Residential Resale Real Estate Purchase Contract published by the Arizona REALTORS® (AAR). That form sets the order of events and most of the deadlines below. Two things to know up front:

  • Days are calendar days. Weekends and holidays count unless the contract says otherwise.
  • The contract also serves as escrow instructions. A title and escrow company, acting as a neutral third party, follows it to close the sale.

Default deadlines can be changed by agreement, and forms are updated from time to time, so always read the version you sign. This guide explains the process in general terms. It isn't legal or lending advice; for those questions, talk with an Arizona real estate attorney or your lender.

Before touring homes with a REALTOR®, you'll sign a written buyer-broker agreement. This became standard practice nationwide in 2024, and Arizona REALTORS® forms reflect it.

There are two common AAR forms:

  • Buyer-Broker Agreement to Show Property. A short, non-exclusive form used for touring. You can sign one with more than one broker.
  • Buyer-Broker Employment Agreement. A fuller agreement that names one broker to represent you through the purchase and spells out duties and terms.

Either way, broker compensation is not set by law. It's negotiated between you and the broker and must be stated as a specific, ascertainable amount. Read the agreement before you sign and ask questions about anything that isn't clear.

Teigh Wade, REALTOR® with HomeSmart Elite Group, HomeSmart, offers mobile buyer consultations: she comes to you to explain the agreement, the process and what to expect.

A pre-approval letter from a lender shows sellers you've been reviewed for a loan amount. In Arizona, the standard purchase contract also lets you attach a pre-qualification form from your lender with your offer.

  • Gather pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements and ID.
  • Ask about loan types, down payment options and estimated closing costs.
  • Ask what your payment would include: principal, interest, property taxes, homeowner's insurance and any HOA dues.

Teigh refers buyers to lenders in her network. She doesn't set or promise interest rates; your lender does that. Once you have a budget, you can start looking with the home search. First-time buyer? See first-time home buyers.

When you find the right home, your agent prepares an offer on the AAR resale contract. It covers:

  • Purchase price and how you'll pay (loan type, down payment).
  • Earnest money amount and form.
  • Close of escrow date.
  • Seller concessions, if any, and which items stay with the house.
  • Addenda, such as an HOA addendum, a solar addendum or a counter offer.

The seller can accept, reject or counter. The contract becomes binding once the seller's signed acceptance is delivered by the deadline written in the offer. That date, contract acceptance, starts most of the clocks that follow.

sections.h2: Step 4: Deposit earnest money and open escrow
sections.html:
Earnest money is a good-faith deposit. After acceptance, it's deposited with the escrow company (or, less often, a broker's trust account), and it's applied toward your purchase at closing.

Whether earnest money is refundable depends on the contract. For example, if you cancel properly within the inspection period, or under the appraisal contingency, the contract generally provides for its return. If a buyer breaches the contract and doesn't cure after notice, the earnest money can be subject to forfeiture. Know your deadlines.

Escrow also orders the title commitment, which shows who owns the property, the liens and easements recorded against it, and what the title insurer won't cover. Under the AAR contract, you have five days after receiving the title commitment to disapprove items.

Wire fraud is a real risk in real estate. Never wire money based on emailed instructions alone. Call the escrow officer at a number you've verified independently before sending funds.

sections.h2: Step 5: Review the SPDS and claims history
sections.html:
The Seller's Property Disclosure Statement (SPDS) is the seller's written disclosure of what they know about the home: ownership, HOA, utilities, the roof, plumbing, pool, solar, past repairs, permits and environmental issues.

  • The seller delivers the SPDS within three days after contract acceptance.
  • The seller provides a five-year insurance claims history (or for the time they've owned the home, if shorter) within five days.
  • You have until the end of the inspection period, or five days after receiving the document, whichever is later, to disapprove.

Read it closely. Items mentioned in the SPDS are good leads for your inspector.

The inspection period is your due-diligence window. Under the AAR contract it's ten days after contract acceptance, unless the parties write in a different number.

During this time you can:

  • Hire a home inspector, and specialists for the roof, pool, HVAC, sewer line or termites (wood-destroying insects) as needed.
  • Get homeowner's insurance quotes and confirm coverage is available.
  • Check the flood zone designation.
  • Review pool barrier rules, if the home has a pool. The seller provides the Arizona Department of Health Services pool notice, and the buyer is responsible for checking state, county and city barrier requirements.
  • Research anything else that matters to you, such as square footage, zoning, nearby planned development or commute routes.

Finish every inspection before you send your repair request. The contract expects all disapproved items in one notice.

The Buyer's Inspection Notice and Seller's Response (BINSR) is the AAR form you use before the inspection period ends. On it, you choose one of three paths:

  1. Accept the premises as they are.
  2. Cancel the contract (earnest money is generally returned when you cancel properly within the inspection period).
  3. List items you disapprove of and give the seller a chance to correct them.

If you list items, the seller has five days to respond. The seller may agree, refuse, or offer an alternative such as a credit. A seller who doesn't respond in time is treated as refusing. If the seller doesn't agree to everything, you have five days to cancel or accept the seller's response. If you don't cancel in that window, you're agreeing to close without the items the seller declined. Verbal conversations don't extend these deadlines; only a signed written agreement does.

sections.h2: Step 8: Appraisal and loan status updates
sections.html:
If you're financing, your lender orders an appraisal to confirm the home's value supports the loan.

  • Appraisal contingency. If the property doesn't appraise for at least the purchase price, the AAR contract gives you five days after notice of the appraised value to cancel and have earnest money returned. If you don't cancel in time, the contingency is generally waived. Buyers and sellers may also renegotiate the price.
  • Loan application. You provide basic information to your lender and authorize a credit check within three days of acceptance.
  • Loan Status Update (LSU). Your lender completes the AAR Loan Status Update form, which goes to the seller within ten days after contract acceptance and is updated as the loan progresses.
  • Stay steady. Avoid new debt, large unexplained deposits or job changes during escrow without talking to your lender first.

Many Arizona homes are in a planned community or condominium association. When there's an HOA, escrow notifies the association of the sale. Under state law, an association with 50 or more units delivers its resale disclosure package within ten days after receiving notice; in smaller associations, the seller provides it.

The package includes the CC&Rs, bylaws and rules, current budget, dues and special assessments, recent board minutes, the reserve study if there is one, any pending lawsuits, and any unresolved violations on the home. Read it with these questions in mind:

  • What are the dues, and what do they cover?
  • Are there rules on parking, rentals, exterior changes, solar or pets that affect your plans?
  • Are any special assessments planned?
  • Are there transfer or capital fees due at closing?

If something in the documents is a concern, raise it with your agent right away so it can be addressed within your contract deadlines.

Before closing, you walk through the home to confirm agreed repairs were made and the property is in substantially the same condition as when the contract was accepted. The seller provides receipts for agreed repairs at least three days before close of escrow, and the seller keeps all utilities on through closing so you can test everything.

Arizona REALTORS® recommends doing the walkthrough at least three days before the scheduled closing so any problem can be addressed. Run faucets, test the AC, open the garage door, check appliances and look at the items listed on the BINSR. Skipping an allowed walkthrough can limit your options if you find a problem later.

A few days before closing, you sign your loan and closing documents with the escrow officer or a mobile notary. Federal rules require your lender to give you a Closing Disclosure at least three business days before you sign the loan, so you can compare it with your Loan Estimate.

Deeds and vesting

The AAR resale contract calls for the seller to convey title by warranty deed. Other Arizona deed types you may hear about include the special warranty deed, the quitclaim deed, the disclaimer deed (used when a spouse disclaims an interest) and the beneficiary deed, which lets an owner name who receives the property at death. You'll also choose how to hold title, called vesting. Vesting has legal and tax effects, so ask an attorney or tax professional; escrow officers and agents can't advise you on that choice.

Before closing, you'll wire or deliver your closing funds to escrow. Confirm the wiring instructions by phone at a verified number.

On closing day, the lender funds the loan, escrow confirms all conditions are met, and the deed and deed of trust are sent to the county recorder. In the West Valley, that's the Maricopa County Recorder (or Yavapai County for parts of Wickenburg's surrounding area).

Close of escrow happens when the deed is recorded. Under the standard contract, that's also when you get possession and keys, unless you agreed otherwise in writing. Then it's time to set up utilities in your name and move in.

faqs.q: Do I need to sign an agreement before touring homes in Arizona?
faqs.a: Yes. REALTORS® now need a signed written agreement with a buyer before touring a home. Arizona REALTORS® offers a short, non-exclusive agreement to show property and a fuller buyer-broker employment agreement. Broker compensation isn't set by law; it's negotiated between you and the broker and must be a specific amount. Read the agreement carefully and ask questions before signing.

faqs.q: How long is the inspection period in Arizona?
faqs.a: The standard Arizona REALTORS® resale contract sets the inspection period at ten days after contract acceptance, unless the buyer and seller agree to a different number of days. Days are calendar days. During that time you can complete inspections, research insurance and flood zone, review the SPDS, and deliver a BINSR to accept, cancel or ask for repairs.

faqs.q: What happens after I submit a BINSR?
faqs.a: The seller has five days to respond. They can agree to correct the items, refuse, or propose something else, such as a credit. If they don't respond, they're treated as refusing. If the seller doesn't agree to everything, you then have five days to cancel or accept the response. If you don't cancel, you're agreeing to close without the items the seller declined.

faqs.q: Is earnest money refundable in Arizona?
faqs.a: It depends on why and when the contract is canceled. Under the AAR contract, earnest money is generally returned when a buyer cancels properly under a contingency, such as within the inspection period or the appraisal contingency window. It can be at risk if a buyer breaches the contract and doesn't cure after notice. Talk with an attorney about a specific situation.

faqs.q: What is a Loan Status Update?
faqs.a: The Loan Status Update, or LSU, is an Arizona REALTORS® form your lender fills out to show where your loan stands, such as whether you've been approved and which conditions remain. Under the standard contract, it's delivered to the seller within ten days after contract acceptance and updated as the loan moves forward, so everyone can track progress toward closing.

faqs.q: What if the home appraises below the purchase price?
faqs.a: If your contract includes the appraisal contingency and the home appraises below the purchase price, you have five days after notice of the appraised value to cancel and have your earnest money returned. If you don't cancel in time, the contingency is generally waived. Buyers and sellers can also renegotiate the price or terms. Your lender can explain how the value affects your loan.

faqs.q: When is a home officially sold in Arizona?
faqs.a: Close of escrow happens when the deed is recorded with the county recorder. Before that, the buyer and seller sign their documents with escrow, the lender funds the loan, and escrow confirms all conditions are met. Under the standard contract, the buyer gets possession and keys at close of escrow unless the parties agreed to a different date in writing.

faqs.q: What kind of deed is used in an Arizona home sale?
faqs.a: The standard Arizona REALTORS® resale contract calls for the seller to convey title by warranty deed. Other Arizona deed types include the special warranty deed, quitclaim deed, disclaimer deed and beneficiary deed, each used in different situations. How you take title, called vesting, has legal and tax effects, so it's best to ask an attorney or tax professional before closing.
